summary: Describes how SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3 can coexist, so that systems using different versions of the management framework can work together. It obsoletes RFC 1908 and RFC 2089 and was replaced by RFC 3584.

eli5.summary: Old and new versions of the network-monitoring language need to work together. This explains how they can talk without confusion.

subtitle: How SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3 devices and tools can live side by side on one network.

tldr.problem: Networks ran three versions of the SNMP management framework at once, and their MIB formats, error codes, data types and trap formats do not line up.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2576 gives rules for converting MIB modules from SMIv1 to SMIv2, translating notification parameters both ways, handling mixed versions in multi-lingual agents and proxies, and mapping community strings into SNMPv3 access control.
tldr.outcome: It obsoleted RFC 1908 and RFC 2089 and was itself replaced by RFC 3584.

today: RFC 2576 has been obsoleted by RFC 3584, which is the later coexistence document. It had itself replaced RFC 1908 and RFC 2089.

sections.title: The Three Frameworks and the Four Coexistence Topics
sections.content:
RFC 2576 describes coexistence between version 3 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework (SNMPv3), version 2 (SNMPv2) and the original framework (SNMPv1). It obsoletes RFC 1908 and RFC 2089.

It covers four things: converting MIB documents between SMIv1 and SMIv2 formats, mapping notification parameters, approaches to coexistence in a multi-lingual network (multi-lingual agents and proxies), and the SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c message processing and community-based security models that plug SNMPv1 into the View-Based Access Control Model.

The document separates SNMPv1 access to MIB data from SNMPv2 access to MIB data. SNMPv1 access never generates exception codes or uses the Counter64 type, while SNMPv2 access may do both and never generates readOnly, noSuchName or badValue errors. A multi-lingual implementation may implement all access as SNMPv2 and translate for SNMPv1 requests.
sections.eli5: There are three versions of the same language, and some devices speak only one. This document is the phrasebook that lets them understand each other.

sections.title: Converting MIB Modules from SMIv1 to SMIv2
sections.content:
MIB modules written in SMIv1 may keep being used with protocol versions that use SNMPv2 PDUs. To make a module conform to SMIv2, a list of changes is required. The IMPORTS must reference SNMPv2-SMI, and the MODULE-IDENTITY macro must follow immediately. Unbounded INTEGER becomes Integer32 (or gets a range), Counter becomes Counter32, and Gauge becomes Gauge32 or Unsigned32.

The ACCESS clause becomes MAX-ACCESS, a STATUS of mandatory or optional becomes current, deprecated or obsolete, and every object needs a DESCRIPTION. Objects must be gathered into OBJECT-GROUPs, and trap definitions become NOTIFICATION-TYPE definitions: the ENTERPRISE clause is removed, VARIABLES is renamed OBJECTS, and notifications are collected into NOTIFICATION-GROUPs.

Standards-track modules also need a MODULE-COMPLIANCE statement, and the old capabilities macro is replaced by AGENT-CAPABILITIES. Converting a module does not by itself require deprecating its objects.
sections.eli5: It is like updating an old recipe card to a new standard layout. The dish stays the same, but the headings and measurements are rewritten so everyone reads them the same way.

sections.title: Translating Notification Parameters
sections.content:
SNMPv1 traps and SNMPv2 notifications carry different parameters, so they must be translated when an entity sends in a format other than the one it generated, or when a proxy forwards between versions. SNMPv1 uses enterprise, agent-addr, generic-trap, specific-trap, time-stamp and a variable-binding list. SNMPv2 uses sysUpTime, snmpTrapOID and the remaining variable bindings.

Going from v1 to v2, the time-stamp becomes sysUpTime. A generic-trap of enterpriseSpecific(6) gives an snmpTrapOID made of the enterprise value plus 0 and the specific-trap number, while generic-trap values 0 to 5 map to the standard traps from RFC 1907. A proxy also appends snmpTrapAddress.0, snmpTrapCommunity.0 and snmpTrapEnterprise.0 bindings so the original agent address, community and enterprise are not lost.

Going from v2 to v1 reverses this. If the variable bindings contain a Counter64 object, the notification cannot be encoded in an SNMPv1 packet and cannot be sent using SNMPv1.
sections.eli5: A trap is a device shouting that something happened. The two versions fill in the shouting form differently, so this explains how to copy the answers from one form to the other without losing any.

sections.title: Multi-lingual Agents and Proxies
sections.content:
There are two approaches. Multi-lingual implementations speak several SNMP versions and use the one both sides support. Proxy implementations translate between versions for elements that each speak only one.

For multi-lingual command responders, a Counter64 value must never appear in a response to an SNMPv1 request. Such objects are treated as not in view, so a v1 GetRequest for one gets noSuchName, and a v1 GetNextRequest skips them. SNMPv2 exceptions (noSuchObject, noSuchInstance and endOfMibView) are converted into a noSuchName error with the error-index pointing at the offending variable binding. A command generator must downgrade a GetBulk request to GetNext when using SNMPv1.

Proxies follow similar rules. When forwarding a GetBulkRequest-PDU over SNMPv1 they change it to a GetNextRequest-PDU, and an InformRequest-PDU can only be forwarded with SNMPv2c or SNMPv3. The RFC also notes that a proxy re-sending GetNext requests to skip Counter64 objects can be expensive.
sections.eli5: Some translators speak every version, and some go-betweens pass messages from a speaker of one version to a listener of another. Either way, anything the old version cannot say gets turned into a polite error.

sections.title: Community Strings and the SNMP-COMMUNITY-MIB
sections.content:
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c identify a requester by a community string, not by the user-based model of SNMPv3. To plug them into the common architecture, RFC 2576 defines the SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c message processing models (message processing model value 0 for SNMPv1 and 1 for SNMPv2c) and the community-based security models (security model 1 and 2), always at security level noAuthNoPriv.

The SNMP-COMMUNITY-MIB maps in both directions between a community name and a securityName, contextEngineID and contextName. Its snmpCommunityTable is searched in lexicographic order. A row matches an incoming request when the community string equals snmpCommunityName and, if a transport tag is set, the source address matches the tagged snmpTargetAddrTable entries. If no row matches, authentication fails and snmpInBadCommunityNames is incremented. The MIB also adds a transport address mask, snmpTargetAddrTMask, and a maximum message size, snmpTargetAddrMMS.
sections.eli5: A community string is like a club password. This part turns that password into a proper membership card so the newer, stricter access rules can decide what each member may see.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 provide no security of their own. Mapping community names into securityName and contextName lets view-based access control limit what unsecured operations can reach, and the RFC says it is important for administrators to use this capability.

The SNMP-COMMUNITY-MIB could expose community strings that give access to more than the usual public community, so a security administrator may wish to make it inaccessible to that community. A proxy that translates between SNMPv1 or SNMPv2c and SNMPv3 can also lose security: an SNMPv3 message with authentication and privacy that is forwarded over SNMPv1 loses those protections, which calls for careful proxy configuration, perhaps with an encrypted tunnel.
sections.eli5: The old versions have no real locks, so you must add your own. And if a safe message is passed along using an old version, it loses its lock on the way.
